source.title: Toward Identifiable Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: Walter Nelson; Theofanis Karaletsos; Francesco Locatello

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures run-to-run stability of SAE dictionaries and codes, challenging the idea that learned SAE features are invariably stable units while showing that stability improves in some settings and model variants.
record.gate_note: The paper tests SAE run-to-run dictionary and code stability (V5), not superposition geometry, polysemanticity, feature capacity competition, or whether SAE features are complete or canonical. Table 1 and Table 2 provide the extracted stability metrics. Reconstruction error, aRIP scores, and Table 3 downstream benchmarks are not rows because they do not directly measure the stability claim.
record.test_reason: The paper measures run-to-run stability of SAE dictionaries and codes across seeds, on synthetic data and on Pythia-160M and DINOv2 activations. It also gives a theorem that dictionary stability does not imply code stability. Both bear directly on the 'stable units' part of V5. Standard TopK SAEs are found unstable. The study's own variants (iSAE, iSAE-ME) improve stability on synthetic data but not fully on real activations.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that standard TopK SAEs are not identifiable (stable) across training runs, and that dictionary stability (DCS) does not imply code stability. Bidirectional features, aRIP regularization and a multistep encoder improve stability, near-perfectly on synthetic data. On real Pythia/DINOv2 activations code stability remains far from perfect, and the multistep encoder worsens it. They caution that stability does not establish recovery of a ground-truth representation.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates SAE dictionary and code identifiability rather than reproducing Toy Models of Superposition. It compares TopK, AbsTopK, aRIP-regularized iSAE, and multistep-encoder iSAE-ME; it does not implement the original toy-network method.
record.method_sensitivity: Results differ by data regime and SAE variant. The multistep encoder improves synthetic identifiability but worsens dictionary and code identifiability on Pythia-160M and DINOv2 activations; AbsTopK gives the highest dictionary stability on both real activation datasets.
record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: The authors note a gap between synthetic data and real-world activations, report only TopK-style SAE experiments, and say real-setting code stability remains far from perfect. No uncertainty estimates are stated for the stability metrics. The paper also says its results do not establish recovery of a particular ground-truth data-generating process.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant Table 1 or Table 2 run-to-run dictionary/code stability results were omitted. Reconstruction error, aRIP measurement, and Table 3 downstream benchmark outcomes were left out because they do not directly measure V5 stability.

untested.parts: Completeness, canonicality and faithfulness of SAE features to the model's own units. The authors state that run-to-run stability does not show recovery of a ground-truth representation.
Toy-model superposition geometry, sparsity-dependent phase transitions and regular geometry are not studied.
The capacity-competition account of polysemanticity is not studied.
Non-capacity causes of polysemanticity are not studied.
SAEs are trained on Pythia and DINOv2, but whether real-model features are distributed or truly sparse is not tested.
Whether superposed features are one-dimensional or multi-dimensional is not tested.

missing.what: Oracle (OMP) code identifiability on each learned dictionary. It shows a stable dictionary does not by itself yield stable codes, and that on real data the oracle is weaker than the SAE encoder.
missing.locator: Table 1 and Table 2, Oracle IoU/ℓ2 columns; Sections 4.1-4.2

missing.what: Theorem 3.2: a fixed, well-reconstructing dictionary can admit distinct continuous encoders with different sparsity patterns. Codes are thus non-identifiable even when the dictionary is stable.

record.verdict_notes: Run-to-run stability is a necessary part of V5, not the whole of it. The record misaligns the Table 2 DINOv2 columns: six numbers are printed per row, with MSE or RS in a stray column. Correct SAE IoU/ℓ2 values are TopK 0.519/0.442, AbsTopK 0.524/0.424, iSAE 0.585/0.372 and iSAE-ME 0.356/0.451; these match the text's qualitative claims. No seed counts or uncertainty are reported.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not test feature overlap, near-orthogonal geometry, sparsity-dependent transitions, or regular geometry in toy networks.
It does not test whether polysemanticity arises from capacity competition or whether more important features receive dedicated dimensions.
It does not test other causes of polysemanticity or whether polysemanticity is evidence of superposition.
The paper trains SAEs on Pythia and DINOv2 activations, but does not test whether real-model features are spread across neurons or whether an SAE recovers underlying sparse features.
It measures run-to-run dictionary and code stability, but does not establish that SAE features are complete, canonical, or faithful units of the underlying model representation.
It treats dictionary atoms as vectors but does not test whether underlying superposed features are one-dimensional rather than multidimensional.
